items.q: Match the following DKA feature — 1) Trigger 2) Anion gap 3) Potassium 4) Plasma glucose … A) Infection, MI, missed insulin, pregnancy, cocaine B) Raised with positive ketones C) Total body depletion despite normal/raised serum K+ D) 250–600 mg/dL
items.exp: Triggers include infection, MI, missed insulin, pregnancy and cocaine; AG is raised with positive ketones; total body K+ is depleted despite serum K+ often being normal/raised; plasma glucose is typically 250–600 mg/dL. (Book p930)

items.q: A patient on insulin has a chest infection and develops Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain and plasma glucose 380 mg/dL with ketones. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.exp: Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, glucose 380 mg/dL with ketones fit DKA, often precipitated by infection. (Book p930)

items.q: Assess DKA: I Insulin deficiency causes lipolysis and ketogenesis. II Hepatic ketogenesis is stimulated by glucagon excess.
items.exp: Insulin deficiency and glucagon excess together drive lipolysis, FFA delivery to liver, and ketogenesis producing β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. (Book p930)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature more typical of HHS than DKA?
opts: Severe hyperglycaemia >600 mg/dL with profound dehydration
items.exp: Positive serum ketones is a feature of DKA, not HHS; HHS has severe hyperglycaemia, high osmolarity and minimal ketosis. (Book p930)

items.q: The dominant ketone body in DKA is ___.
items.exp: β-hydroxybutyrate predominates in DKA; standard urine dipstick detects acetoacetate preferentially and may underestimate the true ketone load. (Book p930)

items.q: Match the following DKA workup — 1) Glucose 2) Electrolytes 3) ABG 4) Serum osmolality … A) 250–600 mg/dL B) K+ depletion, Na+ artefact C) pH <7.3, HCO3 <15 D) 300–320 mOsm/kg
items.exp: Glucose typically 250–600 mg/dL; electrolytes show K+ depletion and pseudohyponatraemia; ABG shows pH <7.3 and HCO3 <15; serum osmolarity 300–320 mOsm/kg. (Book p930)

items.q: A DKA patient has serum Na+ 128 mEq/L and glucose 540 mg/dL. The corrected sodium is approximately:
items.exp: Corrected Na+ ≈ measured Na+ + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100. With glucose 540, correction ≈ 128 + 7 ≈ 135 mEq/L. (Book p930)

items.q: Assess potassium in DKA: I Initial serum K+ may be normal or high. II Insulin will further drop K+; replacement is needed.
items.exp: Total body K+ is depleted even when initial serum K+ is normal/high; insulin therapy will lower K+ and replacement is required. (Book p930)

items.q: Match the following DKA investigation to its expected finding — 1) Urine dipstick 2) β-hydroxybutyrate 3) Lactate 4) Anion gap … A) Ketones positive (acetoacetate) B) Elevated (best ketone) C) May be elevated if shock D) Raised (>10)
items.exp: Urine dipstick detects acetoacetate; β-hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone; lactate may rise with shock; anion gap is raised >10. (Book p930)

items.q: A patient with new T1DM has glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.18, HCO3 10 mEq/L and K+ 5.6 mEq/L. The first hour of management is most consistent with:
opts: IV fluids, hold insulin until K+ checked, monitor
items.exp: Fluids and insulin are cornerstones; insulin should be withheld if K+ <3.3 until replacement; bicarbonate is not routine. (Book p930)

items.q: The anion gap is calculated as Na+ − (Cl− + ___).
items.exp: AG = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−); the alternative including K+ is seldom used clinically. (Book p930)

items.q: Assess DKA triggers: I New-onset T1DM can present with DKA. II Pregnancy predisposes to DKA.
items.exp: New-onset T1DM commonly presents with DKA; pregnancy increases susceptibility because of hormonal changes. (Book p930)
